papers.title: Generalized PINN-Based Inverse Estimation of Spatially Varying Heat Transfer Coefficients with Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: This study investigates generalized boundary representations and transfer learning for physics-informed neural-network (PINN) estimation of spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling. Piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators are inferred from transient interior-temperature measurements and evaluated against CFD-CHT reference HTC profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000 and 15000. A discrete Adjoint-FEM formulation with gradient regularization based on the $H^1$-seminorm provides an independent inverse-method comparison. Transfer learning is investigated under two source-target conditions: transfer between noise levels at the same Reynolds number, and transfer from a controlled Gaussian-profile problem to CFD-CHT-derived target problems at different Reynolds numbers. For the representative Re = 5000 target with 5% measurement noise, quadratic, PWL, and neural-network PINNs achieve relative HTC-profile errors of 5.08, 5.31 and 5.19%, respectively, while generalized representations reduce the error for the Re = 15000 target from 16.76% for the quadratic PINN to 14.41% and 14.46%. Transfer learning reduces target-training time by 57.86-81.71% for fixed-Reynolds-number transfer and by 50.59-84.94% for Gaussian-to-CHT transfer. Its effect on reconstruction accuracy is target dependent: fixed-profile PWL transfer remains within 0.30 percentage points of scratch training, whereas Gaussian-to-CHT transfer produces differences of 0.10-1.52 percentage points across targets and representations. These results demonstrate that generalized PINN representations can accommodate spatially varying HTC profiles without a prescribed quadratic form, while transfer learning can substantially reduce target-training cost for repeated inverse estimation, with the resulting reconstruction accuracy depending on source-target compatibility.

papers.title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
papers.abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

papers.title: Space-Time Parallel Direct Numerical Simulation of Rayleigh-B\'enard Convection
papers.abstract: Rayleigh-B\'enard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.

papers.title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
papers.abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.

papers.title: acousticHelmholtzFoam: an MPI-parallel unstructured finite-volume solver for frequency-domain acoustics in heterogeneous two-phase media with perfectly matched layers
papers.abstract: acousticHelmholtzFoam is an OpenFOAM application that computes time-harmonic acoustic pressure fields in heterogeneous gas-liquid media on unstructured polyhedral meshes. The complex pressure is stored as real and imaginary volume fields, the material coefficients are constructed from a volume-of-fluid phase fraction with geometric face-fraction averaging, and open boundaries are truncated by Cartesian perfectly matched layers (PMLs) whose damping tensor is generated by the companion utility setPMLFields. The two coupled real-valued equations are discretized with the cell-centred finite-volume operators of OpenFOAM and assembled explicitly, including processor couplings and boundary contributions, into a distributed PETSc matrix that is solved by default with the MUMPS sparse direct solver. The solver writes pressure amplitude, complex velocity, acoustic radiation pressure and time-averaged momentum flux for acoustic-force evaluation. This paper documents the implemented equations, the case interface, the assembly and solution algorithm, the build procedure and the test infrastructure. A layered gas-liquid-PML case with an analytical solution serves as an end-to-end regression: on 8000 cells the whole-domain relative complex-pressure error is $1.197\times10^{-3}$, and serial and MPI solutions on up to eight ranks agree to within $10^{-12}$ in relative $L_2$ norm. A single-axis acoustic-levitator height sweep with constant-volume spheroidal drops demonstrates the two-phase material input and the force output, and strong- and problem-size-scaling measurements characterize the direct-solver workflow. The numerical formulation and its verification are presented in a companion paper (arXiv:2610.01593).

papers.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
papers.abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

papers.title: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method for the shallow water equations on Cartesian grids: mass conservation and wetting and drying over variable topography
papers.abstract: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method is proposed for the two-dimensional shallow water equations with a variable bed (topography), solved with an explicit Godunov-type finite volume scheme (unsplit second-order MUSCL, HLLC flux, hydrostatic reconstruction) on Cartesian grids. Ghost-cell methods leak mass through the wall. To find a robust and conservative treatment, eight constructions of the ghost values and a cut-cell form of the continuity equation were applied to seven test problems, which include wetting and drying on sloping beds and a laboratory dam break. In the resulting scheme, the ghost values are interpolated bilinearly at the image point; solid and dry nodes are excluded, and the weights of the remaining nodes are renormalized. Mass is conserved by solving the continuity equation in cut-cell form, while the momentum equations are left unchanged. The proposed scheme is about as accurate as the ghost-cell method without this modification and preserves a lake at rest whose shoreline crosses an immersed wall. Because only the continuity equation is modified, it avoids the treatment of the momentum equations on cut cells (wall pressure, cell merging) that a full cut-cell method requires.

papers.title: One-way pressure-independent valves with hysteresis and chattering
papers.abstract: We propose a model for the one-dimensional isothermal gas flow through a valve in a pipe. The valve aims at keeping the outgoing flow in an assigned interval; moreover, its opening and closing depend on a further parameter. The model is realized by a system of two conservation laws with suitable conditions coupling the ingoing and the outgoing flow. We study the corresponding Riemann problem, where non-classical shocks show up. Although simple, the model allows to study two key oscillatory behaviors of the flow, which are due, respectively, to the chattering of the valve, especially seen in the numerical simulations, and to the stabilizing hysteresis induced by the valve operation. We characterize the states leading to chattering and show how they depend on the parameters of the model. Through several numerical simulations, we study the interplay between the two above phenomena.

papers.title: Philip L. Roe, the British Scientist. The Cranfield Years and Beyond
papers.abstract: Philip L. Roe, the renowned British scientist, passed away on April 26, 2026, at the age of 87, while Professor Emeritus at the University of Michigan. My association with Phil Roe began in 1984, when he joined the Cranfield Institute of Technology, UK, as Professor of Computational Fluid Dynamics, while I was a postdoctoral research fellow at the same institution. For more than four decades, his incisive ideas, physical principles and distinctive approach to research on numerical methods for solving hyperbolic partial differential equations have had a lasting influence on my own approach to research in the field. Here I recount some personal memories and anecdotes emerging from the rewarding experience of interacting with Phil during the Cranfield years and beyond. I also review, quite succinctly in places, some of the main research topics that he pursued throughout much of his academic career. These notes are intended as a modest homage to Roe's impact on the subject, as well as to his influence on the careers of generations of scientists in both academia and industry.

papers.title: SIREN: A nonlinear Rankine-source boundary element solver for the stationary motion of a marine vehicle in calm water
papers.abstract: SIREN (Ship Inviscid Resistance and Elevation eNgine) is a Rankine-source panel solver for the steady wave resistance of a ship, in the tradition of Dawson's method. The free-surface condition is linearised about a base flow, and the linearisation is iterated. In the present formulation the base flow is the solution of a Neumann problem on the actual boundary: sources on the entire hull, wet and dry, and on the free surface panels, with impermeability imposed on both, so that the free surface acts as a rigid lid at the position it currently occupies. This replaces the classical double-body flow, whose image about z=0 is meaningful only for a flat surface and a hull cut at z=0, and it removes the need for desingularised free-surface panels. In the non-linear iteration the free-surface panels are moved rigidly in the vertical to the relaxed wave elevation at their centroid, the hull panels are marked wet or dry against the moved surface, and the base flow is recomputed on the moved geometry; impermeability applies to the whole hull regardless of this marking, which is used only to select which panels enter the force integral, and under-relaxation is confined to the passes where the non-linear correction accumulates without being reset. The radiation condition is imposed by a one-row upstream shift of the collocation points, and the wave resistance is obtained by pressure integration and, independently, by transverse wave-cut analysis.

papers.title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation
papers.abstract: For the first time, we study the effects of mass transfer on alloy droplet impact, solidification, and solute non-homogeneity or MacroSegregation (MS). For this purpose, a multi-physics model, including fully-coupled hydrodynamics of multiphase flow, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer, is established and validated carefully across several benchmarks. In addition, a concentration-flux-correction algorithm is proposed to conserve the solute mass within the droplet at the numerical discretization level. The validated model is subsequently used to explore the impact and solidification of an alloy droplet. The results show that accounting for mass transfer and solute transport improves the prediction of the dynamics of a solidifying splat, in a consistent manner with experimental observations, while this effect has been neglected in all previous studies. The analysis demonstrates that this improvement results from the flow sensitivity to the mushy region thickness, which is regulated by local solute concentration through the solidus and liquidus temperatures. Furthermore, analyses of the MS map identify several critical segregation regions most susceptible to defect initiation, such as cracking, including a long negatively segregated vein within the lamella, formed by the severe advective flow through the mush in the middle stages of the impact, a positively segregated region near the rim of the splat, appearing as a result of hook formation, and a major positively segregated zone at the top of the rim, which develops following the accumulation of the solute-rich melt sustained by washout from the lamella.

papers.title: Planar intrusions from a narrow, jet-like source in a linearly stratified ambient
papers.abstract: We present two and three dimensional direct numerical simulations of planar intrusions injected from a continuously supplied, narrow source into a linearly stratified ambient at the level of neutral buoyancy. The evolution passes through three phases. A laminar leading vortex dipole first advances at constant speed with a varicose wave train behind it; the trailing jet then undergoes a sinuous instability whose initial growth rate and wavelength agree with inviscid unstratified planar-jet theory evaluated on the local jet; the flow finally relaxes into a buoyancy-controlled wedge whose area grows linearly in time. Three-dimensional simulations show that the transition remains organized by the planar instability, while three-dimensionality reshapes the near-source region into a slowly evolving, actively mixing zone that entrains an additional twenty to one hundred percent of the source flux depending on source width. Rescaled with this measured effective flux, the downstream intrusion collapses reasonably well onto the similarity solution for a wide-source intrusion.

papers.title: Extension of a mathematical analogy between vortical flows without surface tension and irrotational capillary flows
papers.abstract: In a recent paper, a mathematical analogy was found between two physically distinct classes of two-dimensional free boundary problems in inviscid fluid mechanics. One class involves free surface flows with constant vorticity in the bulk but without boundary surface tension, the other comprises free surface flows without vorticity in the bulk but with non-zero boundary surface tension (capillarity). Several examples were given of pairs of physically-distinct free boundary problems that amount to solving the same mathematical problem, albeit with the possibility of a single constraint arising for the capillary flows. The present work shows that this analogy extends to another pair of physically-distinct problems: a hollow vortex equilibrium in a shear flow with a third order irrotational strain and a steady bubble with surface tension in a simple straining flow. For both problems, we construct an isolated exact solution when a parameter $\gamma=0$ and provide numerical solutions for non-zero $\gamma$. An interesting feature is that non-trivial conformal mapping identities emerge from the class of problems with capillarity that apply equally for the hollow vortex problems when the parameters are appropriately constrained.

papers.title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.

papers.title: Interaction of eccentricity tide and convection
papers.abstract: Aim. We try to understand the interaction of eccentricity tide and convection in icy satellites. Method. We use the numerical calculation of rotating convection with eccentricity tide in a spherical shell. Results. We have the following results. (1) Energy scaling exponent about buoyancy force (or tidal force) decreases with increasing tidal force (or buoyancy force). (2) The combined tide-convection flow is not identical to superposition of two pure flows in respect of energy spectrum. (3) Tide controls large-scale of fluid motion but convection is important for small scale, and the mode-mode transition occurs at intermediate scales. (4) Tide suppresses heat transport efficiency. (5) Dissipation of kinetic energy scales as square of tidal force with a very weak dependence on buoyancy force, which has little impact on dissipation but suppresses the tidal influence on dissipation.

papers.title: Grand minima and intermittency in near-critical convection-driven dynamos
papers.abstract: Context: Solar magnetism exhibits long-term variations on timescales of decades to centuries. Aims: The main aim is to study how the supercriticality of the dynamo affects the variability of magnetic fields on timescales relevant to the Sun. Methods: Three-dimensional rotating magnetohydrodynamic simulations in a spherical wedge geometry are used to produce self-consistent convection-driven dynamos. The supercriticality of the dynamo is controlled by varying the magnetic diffusivity. Results: The main result is that long-term variability of the dynamo increases with decreasing supercriticality of the dynamo and that cases nearest to the onset of dynamo action show extended grand minima-like periods of low activity. The simulations fall in three classes where the least supercritical cases show the largest variations of magnetic activity and where the flow including differential rotation is almost unaffected by the magnetic field. In the cases with the highest supercriticality the magnetic field is permanently strong and differential rotation permanently quenched, both having relatively little temporal variation. In an intermediate regime both the magnetic fields and differential rotation exhibit strong anticorrelated fluctuations. Conclusions: The occurrence of grand minima in the Sun has been conjectured to be due to a weakly supercritical dynamo. The current results support this idea and suggest that the absence of grand minima in earlier global dynamo simulations is because their large-scale dynamos were too supercritical. Furthermore, the current results suggest that the effect of the magnetic field on differential rotation is negligible if the average rms-field is less than about 2~kG.

papers.title: A semi-infinite hydraulic fracture propagating in a poroelastic medium
papers.abstract: We solve the near-tip coupled hydromechanical problem of a hydraulic fracture propagating in a permeable poroelastic medium, represented locally as a semi-infinite crack moving at constant velocity. In the moving tip frame, all fracture fields are steady. The porous solid obeys linear poroelasticity, fracture propagation follows LEFM, fluid flow within the tensile fracture is governed by lubrication theory, and the fracturing and pore fluids are treated as identical Newtonian liquids. The primary unknowns are the fracture opening and the fluid displacement function along the fracture, determined from the resulting non-linear system of equations. In a viscosity--toughness scaling, the problem depends on four dimensionless parameters: a dimensionless permeability $\varrho$ (associated with the intensity of fluid leak-in), a dimensionless effective confining stress $\Sigma_0'$ (measuring the relative importance of fluid leak-off and leak-in), the drained--undrained Poisson's ratio contrast $\beta$, and the poroelastic stress coefficient $\eta$. The solution evolves from a drained, toughness-dominated near-tip asymptote with uniform net pressure to an undrained, storage-viscosity-dominated far-field asymptote. Numerical solutions are obtained over parameter ranges representative of various rock types. The fully coupled model is compared with simplified models, namely uncoupled and one-way coupled formulations, over distances from the fracture front spanning laboratory-to-field scales. The resulting relative difference maps in the $(\varrho,\Sigma_0')$ parameter space identify four characteristic regimes: negligible poroelastic effects, dominance of the direct mechanical poroelastic response, importance of the poroelastic backstress, and a fully coupled regime. The latter occurs mainly at large $\varrho$ and small $\Sigma_0'$, corresponding to strong leak-in relative to leak-off.

papers.title: Generalized Constraint-Controlled Rheological Model: Two Constitutive Pathways under Sinusoidal Periodic Shear Deformation
papers.abstract: We formulate the Generalized Constraint-Controlled Rheological Model (GCCRM) for entangled linear and long-arm-branched polymer melts under sinusoidal periodic shear deformation (SPSD), spanning the linear and strongly nonlinear regimes. Molecular architecture, conformation, chain stretch, flow-active constraints, convective constraint release, dynamic tube dilation, and activated arm retraction define a common upstream molecular state. This state feeds two time-domain constitutive pathways (a configurational stress and a dissipative internal-variable stress) which are recombined before Fourier analysis. For branched polymers, the architecture is described by an entire backbone of molecular weight $M_{bb}$ and $N_a$ long arms of molecular weight $M_a$, with a compliance-weighted representative-constitutive-cell partition. The linear limit is normalized so that the configurational moduli sum to the entanglement modulus, while dynamic tube dilation and stretch drive distinct contributions to dissipative activation. Under reduced closures, GCCRM generates a smooth nonlinear elastic response with an onset of nonlinearity, an approximately logarithmic growth regime, an architecture-dependent maximum, and distinct high-deformation asymptotes. Fourier harmonics, ELR, VLR, and Lissajous curves are treated as post-processing observables of the total stress. The framework establishes a consistent constitutive architecture whose quantitative validation requires one parameter set per material across SPSD and, prospectively, transient shear histories.

papers.title: Evolution of dense liquid marbles under light tapping
papers.abstract: Liquid marbles interface is composed by a dense network of grains trapped by capillarity at their surface. The mix of capillarity and granular character make their interfaces remarkable, allowing non wetting, high mobility and strong robustness which are a basis for numerous applications. A canonical experiment showing out of equilibrium nature of granular material is the so called tapping experiment, where a dry granular medium under vertical vibration reorganize an evolve toward a denser final state function of the vibration amplitude In this paper we explore the out of equilibrium nature of densely covered liquid marbles by measuring their shape, compaction and stresses evolution under vertical vibration. We show that liquid marble do indeed reorganize when submitted to taps, leading to higher internal pressure and lower effective surface tension.

papers.title: Directional Control of Droplet Motion via Geometric Gating
papers.abstract: We explore new methods for inducing the movement of water droplets on elastomeric substrates, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Our approach builds upon the well-known phenomenon that water droplets move easily across these substrates when swelled w,ith silicone oil. While designing shallow open channels and traps on a PDMS film offers a simple way to control a droplet's trajectory by tilting the substrate in two orthogonal directions, this method is poorly suited for manipulating multiple droplets simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce two new methods. The first method utilizes a plano-concave PDMS platform with a radius of curvature significantly larger than the size of the droplet and its translation distance. When the system's configuration is altered, this curved substrate consistently guides the droplet along a curved geodesic. The second method incorporates diode-like gates on the PDMS. These gates are created on either flat or plano-concave PDMS films by embedding thin, rigid plates into the elastomer prior to crosslinking, followed by swelling in silicone oil. This process generates sigmoidal steps that restrict droplet motion to a single direction. Finally, we demonstrate how combining these two strategies enables various forms of directed motion for both single and multiple droplets.

papers.title: Linking Horizontal and Vertical Submesoscale Lagrangian Dynamics South of the Ibiza Channel
papers.abstract: Fronts, eddies, jets, and meanders populate the ocean surface and play a key role in organizing transport and mixing across a wide range of scales. From a Lagrangian perspective, frontal structures are conveniently detected as surface filaments that act as barriers to horizontal transport. However, the degree to which these structures maintain coherence below the surface and the relationship between horizontal and vertical motions in their vicinity remain poorly understood. Here we analyze two such filaments in the western Mediterranean Sea, south of the Ibiza Channel, using a high-resolution ocean simulation and Lagrangian diagnostics specifically designed to characterize submesoscale transport. Backward Finite-Size Lyapunov Exponents (FSLE) computed at successive depths reveal nearly vertical, curtain-like structures extending several tens of meters into the water column, with intensity decreasing with depth. Vertical-velocity sections across the filaments show coherent downward motion aligned with the filament cores, while Lagrangian trajectories indicate rapid horizontal convergence of fluid particles accompanied by sustained downward displacement. The barrier effect of Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCSs) is commonly associated with persistent dynamical features of large-scale flows. Here, however, we demonstrate that FSLE filaments generated by rapidly fluctuating submesoscale dynamics can also act as effective transport barriers. The results demonstrate that the surface signatures of Lagrangian filaments identified through FSLE techniques correspond to three-dimensional transport structures that regulate both lateral aggregation and vertical connectivity in the upper ocean.

papers.title: Preferential concentration of cloud droplets: Coupled effects of phase change and gravitational settling
papers.abstract: Cloud droplets respond to turbulent motion with finite inertia and settle under gravity, while condensation and evaporation change their sizes. The nonuniform accumulation of cloud droplets in turbulent flows, known as preferential concentration, has attracted sustained interest because it affects droplet collision and coalescence rates. We develop an analytical theory that quantifies the coupled effects of droplet inertia, gravitational settling, and phase change on concentration changes. Applying this theory to simulations of two-dimensional homogeneous thermal convection reveals that phase change markedly enhances preferential concentration in this flow, primarily through spatial differences in settling speed. These differences arise because droplets experience different thermodynamic histories along their trajectories and thus acquire different sizes. Droplet transport further increases this settling contribution by rearranging droplets of different sizes. Fluid deformation partly offsets this enhancement by thinning concentration structures, reducing the preferential concentration measured at a fixed spatial scale.

papers.title: Some generalizations of the tornado model
papers.abstract: A possible mechanism of tornado generation is associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability. The supercooled cloud-air mixture near the axis starts to descend and, due to the super adiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated near-surface air mass rises. The complete system of equations for full model includes equations for the stream function, for the azimuthal velocity component, and for the change in density. The refined model considers rotating convection within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics. The simplest model uses a separate equation for the stream function and can be applied to the initial stage of vortex generation. Within the framework of the simplest model, an analytical solution is combined from 8 linear dependencies by height. Rotation increases due to the conservation of angular momentum. Within the framework of the refined model, some unidirectional differential rotation arises, but it depends on boundary conditions (can be local). The full model studies the tornado development as rotating convection from the very beginning to the quasi-stationary stage. Velocity components increase in a coordinated manner. Two cases are considered: a single whirlwind and a two-eyed tornado. Radial flows converge towards the central part of the tornado near the earth surface, and there is an outflow from the "wall" to the axis and to the periphery near the top of the tornado. The maximum vertical velocity component is achieved at a certain radial distance at a certain height. The maximum azimuthal velocity component is achieved in the tornado "wall". Tornado generation criteria are discussed.

papers.title: Causal analysis of inner and outer motions in near-wall turbulence
papers.abstract: In this work, we study the causality of near-wall inner and outer turbulent motions. The inner motions are defined as the self-sustained near-wall cycle, and the outer motions as those living in the logarithmic layer exhibiting footprints on the near-wall region. Causal inference with three typical methods is performed, \emph{i.e.} transfer entropy, information flow, and SURD (synergistic--unique--redundant decomposition of causality). The causal inference methods are first applied to several canonical problems to illustrate their abilities, including a linear problem, a non-linear problem, and a low-dimensional model of near-wall turbulence. It is demonstrated that all three methods can produce consistent causal findings. Furthermore, we study the causalities between the inner and outer turbulent motions in a channel flow using the three methods with an improved inner-outer decomposition method. It is revealed that both the inner and outer motions are causally self-sustained, supporting the self-sustaining mechanism of turbulent motions at all scales. We also find that there are top-down and bottom-up causalities between the outer motions and their near-wall footprints owing to the dynamical coherence of inclined large-scale turbulent motions. More interestingly, pressure is identified to play an active role in the inner-outer causalities and may act as a bridge in linking the inner and outer turbulent motions.

papers.title: On the Two-Dimensional Structure and Asymmetries of Ionic Liquid Electrospray Plumes
papers.abstract: Vacuum electrosprays play important roles in electrospray propulsion, a type of spacecraft electric propulsion wherein charged ions or droplets are accelerated at high velocity to provide spacecraft thrust, and they also have important implications for surface etching and mass spectrometry. Here we present the first fully two-dimensional time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometry survey of a vacuum electrospray plume, generated by a tungsten needle externally-wetted with the ionic liquid 1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate (EMI-BF$_4$). We find that the plume exhibits clear two-dimensional compositional variation, structure, and asymmetry, with heavy particles and energetic neutrals being more prevalent in the center and a ring-shaped distribution for the monomers (the lightest molecular ions) peaking at 10$^\circ$ off beam-axis with a relative minima in the center. Using a new spatial baseline characterization method, we find a population of energetic neutrals firing 3.4$^\circ$ off beam-axis. In particular, we find that by comparing different parts of the plume, the estimated propulsive efficiency from any one sampled point may vary by as much as a factor of 6. We also find that high mass droplets, which are often assumed as absent in many studies of externally-wetted needles, may carry away significant propellant mass at lower effective velocity and reveal a cone-jet mode of operation at 470 nA output current. We thus find that whole-plume compositional surveys may more accurately assess plume composition and propulsive efficiency, and a significant portion of the `missing mass' in electrospray propulsion sources presumed to be operating in the pure ion regime can be potentially explained by limited sampling of the spatially non-uniform ion plume.

papers.title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD
papers.abstract: Setting up, running, and assessing a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation requires substantial manual effort, from meshing and solver setup to diagnosis and interpretation, and repeating it across design variants slows engineering iteration. We present CFD Forge, an agentic framework built around OpenFOAM that carries an engineering request through case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting. A large language model interprets the request, reads the simulation evidence, identifies likely causes of problems, and proposes actions from a closed set. Automation is only useful if its results can be trusted, so acceptance is not left to the model: deterministic checks, registered for each type of flow, measure explicit criteria and decide. We demonstrate the framework on a converging-diverging nozzle and a two-dimensional forward-facing step, including geometry and operating changes requested in text. A turbulent cube, run outside the agent loop, shows why the checks matter: the solver completed and the mean drag settled, but the lateral-force oscillations were still growing, so a retrospective assessment withheld acceptance. To test this separation, we replayed 36 recorded simulation states, some with deliberately altered diagnostics, through the same model in two setups. Judging from the evidence without the check results, the model accepted 12 of the 13 detectable faults in all three repeats; with CFD Forge's checks deciding, none was accepted. The two setups also differ in prompting, and a fixed rule reached the same verdicts, so the model's value lies in the open-ended work rather than the verdict. Case files, recorded model calls, and decisions are retained for audit. A model that does the work, paired with checks that decide what is accepted, is a step toward automated CFD that can be trusted in high-throughput design and active-learning loops.

papers.title: Finding a reconnection in a vortex-haystack
papers.abstract: Counter-rotating vortex reconnection is a topology-transforming event that leads to strong vorticity amplification and is often associated with the most irregular regions of the velocity field. Detecting such events directly in turbulent flows is a major challenge due to the ambiguity inherent in the definition of a vortex and the rapid proliferation of intense small scale vortices. We develop a novel methodology by combining two tools. The first is a local in scale, space and time regularity indicator that isolates spatio-temporal regions of interest. The second is a reconnection indicator that exploits a well-known property of vortex reconnection namely, that the enstrophy (volume integral of the square of vorticity) flows from the symmetry to the collision plane. To examine the flow of enstrophy in the correct reference frame, a new method inspired by orientational order parameters in liquid crystals is developed. We then show a proof of concept for our reconnection indicator by comparing it with diagnostic methods available in the literature. The method is validated on experimental datasets from a turbulent von K\'arm\'an flow at two different resolutions, one of which allows us to probe the flow below the Kolmogorov scale, $\eta$. Our findings suggest that counter-rotating vortex reconnection could be a potential mechanism for the creation of motions at scales below $\eta$.

papers.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
papers.abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/\epsilon$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

papers.title: Surfactant-induced Marangoni stresses and surface viscosity in Faraday instability
papers.abstract: We investigate the influence of insoluble-surfactant elasticity and Boussinesq-Scriven surface viscosity on the parametric instability of an interface separating two viscous fluids. The two-fluid Floquet formulation of Kumar& Tuckerman (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 279, 1994, pp. 49-68) is extended to include surfactant transport, Marangoni stresses and surface viscosity. For the parameter range considered, both mechanisms increase the onset acceleration relative to the clean interface state, but through distinct responses: Marangoni elasticity produces a non-monotonic threshold, whereas surface viscosity yields a monotonic increase towards saturation. Analysis of the corresponding unforced gravity-capillary modes shows that both mechanisms modify modal damping and natural frequency. Wavenumber selection reduces the detuning from subharmonic resonance by approximately an order of magnitude relative to that evaluated at the clean interface critical wavenumber. Along the selected branches, variations in the onset acceleration closely follow those in modal damping, with residual detuning playing a secondary role. Despite their distinct interfacial stress mechanisms, both Marangoni elasticity and surface viscosity suppress tangential interfacial motion in the strong-rheology limit, approaching a common tangentially immobilized condition.

papers.title: Nonlinear waves and conservative transport in soluble-surfactant falling films on compliant substrates
papers.abstract: We investigate finite-amplitude waves in a liquid film containing a soluble surfactant as it flows down an inclined compliant substrate. The coupled motion of the liquid and a spring-backed plate is described by a conservative weighted-residual model, which also accounts for surfactant transport in the bulk and at the free surface. The reduction retains viscous terms arising from wall motion, and its pressure closure recovers fluid added mass under uniform translation. Comparison with the coupled Orr-Sommerfeld problem gives a difference of approximately $1\%$ in the peak growth rate of the film mode at $Re=25$. Nonlinear computations are then used to examine travelling states and their dependence on substrate properties and surfactant coupling. Along the prescribed stiffness-damping path, substrate displacement decreases by more than four orders of magnitude, while wave speed changes by less than $1\%$. The extrema of free-surface elevation and liquid thickness vary differently, so surface height alone does not reliably indicate film thinning over a deformable support. In the cases studied, Marangoni coupling reduces surfactant localisation and weakens the wave and substrate response. Moving-frame reconstruction reveals recirculation near the wave crest and distinguishes propagation of the deformation pattern from transverse substrate motion. The load-work budget identifies capillary pressure as the principal net source of substrate work for the two compliant supports considered. A control calculation in which stiffness is varied at fixed damping shows a substantial change in damping loss but a comparatively small change in deformation.
